Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching mlove Nov 17, 2026 Release DateNovember 17, 2026 DescriptionPurposeCISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.Actions to takeCISA urges organizations to take the following actions:Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.ResourcesCISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:Vendor GuidanceOracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Update – November 2026DisclaimerThe information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”.

It has been revealed that the announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the tech giant first confirmed in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and latest governance tools arriving alongside them.

Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been declared ahead of general availability.

It has been revealed that also confirmed as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a tech giant’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment right now available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”.

Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s new frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he mentioned.

In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft states each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.

The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and customers to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure must still be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will need to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.

Along with the guardrails, Microsoft unveiled what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and MasterCard, to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”.

Sources indicate that along with the other revealed additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft indicates is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”.

Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” stated Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”.

Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he noted. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”.

That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure blueprint.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog chayes Nov 18, 2026 Release DateNovember 18, 2026 DescriptionCISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output VulnerabilityCVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel VulnerabilityCVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection VulnerabilityCVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection VulnerabilityThese types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. #19906. Flipper Zero vs. Flipper One: Why the fresh model isn’t an upgrade

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1114 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Flipper Zero vs. Flipper One: Why the fresh model isn’t an upgrade

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I missed the Flipper Zero Kickstarter in 2020, and I didn’t get my hands on one until 2023.
  • Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.
  • Recent findings suggest that just when I thought I’d reached the limits of what the Zero was capable of, I discovered the world of third-party firmware, which opened the door to even more features and tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I missed the Flipper Zero Kickstarter in 2020, and I didn’t get my hands on one until 2023. Since then, it’s been one of those devices that continually exceed my expectations. It’s the perfect gadget for making the unseen world of point-to-point access-control protocols visible, including sub-GHz radio, NFC, 125kHz RFID, infrared, and iButton. The stuff Flipper calls “Layer 0.”.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.

Recent findings suggest that just when I thought I’d reached the limits of what the Zero was capable of, I discovered the world of third-party firmware, which opened the door to even more features and tools. Over the years, that scene has grown into an active community of developers building all sorts of novel apps for the platform.

In a recent development, by May 2026, Flipper had sold over a million Zero units, and a large community had gathered around the device. When the manufacturer introduced the Flipper One, it made it clear it wasn’t a replacement, but a totally newly introduced device. Comparing the two is like comparing a hammer to a screwdriver, so what are the significant differences?

It has been revealed that the Flipper One is a full Linux computer (running the Debian-based Flipper OS on a mainline Linux kernel) built to work with everything that’s IP-connected: Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and, via M.2 expansion modules, 5G and satellite. If you wanted, you could use the One as a router, a VPN gateway, or a bridge between wired and wireless networks — so-called “layer 1” stuff.

The Zero is one of those rare devices that continually managed to exceed my expectations. It was a small, pocket-sized gadget that made visible the unseen world of point-to-point access-control protocols such as sub-GHz radio, NFC, 125kHz RFID, infrared, and iButton.

It has been revealed that I’ve lent my Zero to youngster, and within a few minutes they’re using it to do real stuff, and they’re learning as they go. Everything is built-in, and Flipper the Dolphin (took me a while to get that) is there to guide you through the steps.

You could easily spend six months running the software on the Zero and working your way through the Lab, Flipper’s free app store, before you’re ready to delve into the third-party firmware options out there.

Also: Heat from your charger could be killing your battery – I found one that stays cool.

And thanks to Flipper selling over a million units, that third-party scene has grown into an active community of developers building all sorts of novel apps for the platform. When you’re ready to make that leap, I suggest starting with Unleashed. This will give you the familiarity of the firmware that came with the Flipper Zero, but add features — such as extending the sub-GHz frequency range by removing geolocation blocks and adding a lot of NFC-related features, and fun things like games.

According to recent reports, you can pick up a Zero now for $169 and be using it to explore the world around you by the end of the week. I’m not saying don’t jump on the Kickstarter and get a One for the special price of $399 (especially considering that once it’s out, it’ll retail for $550), but that unit won’t be in your hands until at least July 2027.

The One is a very different beast to the Zero. While the Zero runs FreeRTOS-based firmware, the One is a full computer powered by the Debian-based Flipper OS on a mainline Linux kernel. This means that the One can have USB, HDMI, and Ethernet ports, and like a PC, it’s expandable thanks to the M.2 slot which supports SSD drives and optional radio modules.

You can even connect a One to a keyboard and external display for a full desktop experience.

While the Zero is the tool for point-to-point access-control protocols where there’s no network, no IP addresses, and no internet involved, the One is for everything IP-connected, such as Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and, by making use of optional M.2 modules, 5G, LoRa, and satellite. This means that you can customize the One to be a network appliance such as a router, VPN gateway, or a bridge between wired and wireless networks.

Also: Flipper Zero: ‘Can you really hack Wi-Fi networks?’ and other questions answered.

Recent findings suggest that being a full computer also means the Wi-Fi will be more capable and fully featured than the Wi-Fi on a laptop. Anything that you can do on a computer, you can do with the One.

Sources indicate that flipper’s aim with the One is “to create a fully upstream-supported ARM computer that never becomes outdated.” To achieve this, Flipper is putting its drivers into mainline Linux rather than building a custom kernel. The One should continue to get kernel updates for a long time to come. But as of right now, the software is unfinished, and it has been asking the community to help finish drivers and core software.

It’s worth pointing out that some have their doubts that Flipper will be able to achieve its goal of no binary blobs, no proprietary drivers, and no vendor-locked board support package, and that there will still be some for things like Wi-Fi and cellular connectivity.

Here’s a comparison chart detailing the differences between the two.

Industry observers note that I wish I could simply recommend one over the other, but it’s not that kind of choice. The real question is whether you need “Layer 0” or “Layer 1” tools, not which Flipper is “better”. You might decide you need both. Full disclosure: I haven’t gotten my hands on a One yet, and the question is — can Flipper make it easy to use?

The Zero wasn’t a success because it was powerful, it was a success because it made an invisible world fun and easy to explore for a relatively small price tag and with almost no learning curve.

Also: I’ve owned 50+ portable power stations – one number matters most for its lifespan.

Sources indicate that the One has been made to a different script. It’s more than twice the price; it’s bulkier, a full Linux machine with a learning curve to match, and you’ll need modules (and probably an external display) to get the most out of it. If Flipper can make network tinkering as friendly as the Zero made radio, it’ll be a hit. If it can’t… well, the One becomes yet another mini-PC. And this question can’t be answered until the One ships.

One thing’s for sure, I can’t wait to get my hands on it.

#19903. Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories

Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA.
  • MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning.
  • In a recent development, “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright claims by way of example in the release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.

MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

In a recent development, “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright claims by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”.

Industry observers note that in an accompanying announcement video, Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”.

Wright noted MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

Sources indicate that since this is 2026, it shouldn’t be surprising that MyMems is making heavy use of generative AI (with a “proprietary behavior engine” on top) to transform your typed-up memories into simulated locales and characters. In the announcement video, Wright praises the “entirely open-ended” AI systems Gallium is using “to extract from the stories and whatnot based upon the memories you put into the game.”.

But Wright’s focus on mining memories for simulation content predates the current generative AI boom. What has now become MyMems started off as Proxi, a mobile simulation that was first revealed in 2018 as “a game of self-discovery, a game where we actually uncover the hidden you.” But after years of pre-production work (as outlined in an excellent Vulture piece earlier this year), Wright’s Gallium Studios finally ran out of funding in late 2024, leading to mass layoffs for the small team and an uncertain future for the project.

In a recent development, now the idea has been revived thanks in large part to a partnership with AI middleware firm Artificial Agency. Until now, that organization has mainly been focused on agentic systems that can create “virtual players” to playtest a game or serve as a partner for human players.

Now, Artificial Agency’s marketing indicates the organization’s AI tool will be used to create “a personal behavior model and a knowledge graph” from players’ memories, drawing some unsettling comparisons to significant tech surveillance.

“Meta knows what you click,” the organization writes. “Netflix knows what you watch. Nobody knows what you remember. MemDNA learns from your memories locally and only with your permission.”.

Wright remarked the partnership with Artificial Agency will let Gallium benefit from “off-the-shelf” AI solutions without having to “become an AI research tech giant” in its own right. He also said the collaboration will help limit costs by providing a cheaper option than the “really expensive” frontier models that might be overkill for a project like this.

“Right now AI has opened a vast new design area and I’m enjoying, you know, exploring that as a designer,” Wright said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, setting up a power station for backup power gives you a profound sense of satisfaction.
  • I’ve reached the stage in my life where I’m a substantial fan of a steady backup system.
  • Also: The best portable power stations of 2026: Expert and lab tested.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, setting up a power station for backup power gives you a profound sense of satisfaction. I imagine it’s how preppers feel when they add to their doomsday hoard. The comfort in knowing your home will remain powered during an outage is unlike any other, especially if you have kids or live in an area that experiences a lot of blackouts.

I’ve reached the stage in my life where I’m a substantial fan of a steady backup system. Because of this, I enjoy testing power stations of all sizes, and I’m lucky enough to review these devices for a living.

Also: The best portable power stations of 2026: Expert and lab tested.

The following power stations are listed in order of units sold, based on the links clicked from ZDNET stories thus far in 2026. (A note: Your privacy is protected — we only have access to aggregate data from our user base, and there is no way for us to identify individual people’s purchases.).

Also: Best early Black Friday deals.

It has been revealed that the EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra X is one of the most powerful power stations that still retains some portability — though that’s saying a lot for 350 pounds. The DPUX can power your whole home with a 12kW to 36kW output and scalable 12 to 180kWh capacity. I have my DPUX as part of a backup power system for my house and keep a DIY solar setup plugged into it with ground-mounted panels.

Review: I powered my 3,000-sq-ft home with an EcoFlow battery in a blackout – here’s how it kept my AC on.

The Delta Pro Ultra was my first whole-home power station, thanks to its portability and modular design. Each battery has 6,144Wh capacity, and you can stack up to five batteries under one inverter.

Review: This power station just kept my lights on during an outage.

The DPU has gone out of stock on Amazon, but the DPUX is a fantastic replacement (and an upgrade).

It has been revealed that though it’s not a power station on its own, this EverExceed 5W solar panel was one of the most popular purchases in the category among readers. This portable panel is designed to power outdoor security cameras that run on rechargeable batteries. It has a 360-degree adjustable bracket and a 9.8-foot cable.

Also: Why I switched to wireless security cameras after years of testing wired models.

Recent findings suggest that jackery makes workhorse power stations that are as versatile as they are reliable. The compact Explorer 1000 v2 is a 1,024Wh battery that can handle 1,500W (3,000W at peak). Aside from being outstanding for camping, this Explorer can handle UPS action, with a 10ms switchover, or become an emergency generator for your home.

Also: The best portable power stations for camping in 2026: Expert tested and reviewed.

The EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra & Smart Home Panel 2 as installed in my garage. / Maria Diaz/ZDNET.

Recent findings suggest that designed to serve as a cohesive smart-home backup system, the EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra works seamlessly with the Smart Home Panel 2. With this setup, you can easily control your circuits from your phone, simply by using the EcoFlow mobile app. You can turn circuits on and off, monitor energy consumption, and customize your backup system’s behavior during an outage, such as prioritizing certain circuits over others.

Also: I found the perfect portable power station for off-grid adventures.

According to recent reports, the Bluetti AC70 is a highly portable unit that offers 768Wh capacity and 1,000W output (2,000W at peak). Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. #19898. Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1581 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
  • When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that customers did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
  • Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that customers did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.

Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.

“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”.

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”.

According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”.

Recent findings suggest that raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output stated, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

Industry observers note that at least one staffer remarked they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance proposal” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with owners in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member mentioned the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

Industry observers note that A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”.

Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

Industry observers note that but Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the complications the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”.

It has been revealed that meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse customers in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten stated was activated without his knowledge.

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.

But Aten stated the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”.

According to recent reports, around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.

According to recent reports, “I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the challenges arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”.

It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton noted. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”.

In a recent development, “We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy concern,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”.

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.

Since Muse debuted in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

Recent findings suggest that but staffers warned Meta that consumers may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

According to recent reports, meta states that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

Sources indicate that that testing “indicated the concern described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse consumers “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta rolled out Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”.

Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been on a quest to minimize my dependence on my Android phone.
  • It has been revealed that then I considered my Android phone’s home screen launcher, which is the window to our mobile digital world.
  • Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been on a quest to minimize my dependence on my Android phone. It started with blocking sensitive information from appearing on my lock screen. The next step was turning off notifications on my lock screen completely. I started feeling more at ease throughout the day. I no longer felt the pull to pick up my phone to see if someone had replied to something, if something happened in the news, or if I missed social media posts.

It has been revealed that then I considered my Android phone’s home screen launcher, which is the window to our mobile digital world. I’d already switched from the default Pixel launcher to Mango Launcher, which I was enjoying and which slightly lessened the distractions. But could a more minimal launcher bring me even more peace?

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

In a recent development, I’d already tried AIO Launcher, and found it to be one of the coolest minimal launchers that I’d ever tried. Then I found three that are even better: Ying Yang Launcher, Olauncher, and Indistractable Minimalist Launcher.

According to recent reports, yin Yang Launcher aims to help you use your phone less, and it does a remarkable job. With Yin Yang Launcher, your Android screen is replaced with two options: basic and minimal. The minimal option is what I chose to focus on, as it breaks the Android display into four pages:.

Sources indicate that if you swipe down from the center of the display, you get a search page, where you can search for installed apps or search the web. Of course, if you swipe down from the top, you get the standard Android Notification Shade.

Long-press the main page to access the settings, where you can customize the home screen, appearance, launcher settings, system settings, and the Mind Space. The Mind Space is a unique feature that serves as a focus mode, where you can select which apps to use and set focus schedules. You can also trigger a manual focus mode and set how long it lasts and which apps are allowed. If you purchase the Pro version of Yin Yang Launcher, you can enable strict mode, which means you cannot disable focus mode until the set time elapses.

Just using Yin Yang Launcher gives me a sense of peace that no other launcher offers.

Also: Changing these 12 settings on my Android phone extended its battery life by hours.

Industry observers note that yin Yang Launcher is free to install from the Google Play Store. There is also a Pro version that adds more features and removes ads. The Pro version is $14.99/yr or $29.99/lifetime.

Industry observers note that I’ve written about Olauncher before. It’s similar to Yin Yang Launcher, without the extra features. With Olauncher, you get a home page with the apps you choose to list; a right swipe opens the phone app, a left swipe opens the camera app, a swipe up opens the full list of apps, and a swipe down opens the Notification Shade.

Long-press the home screen to gain access to the Olauncher Settings, where you can customize the appearance, gestures, the number of apps on the home screen, and a few more options.

Sources indicate that olauncher is about as minimal as it gets. If you want more, you can purchase the Pro version, which adds features like weather, widgets, fonts, folders, AMOLED wallpapers, and more. At the moment, Olauncher Pro is still in early access, so you can use it for free.

Recent findings suggest that indistractable Minimalist Launcher is all about digital detox, and it does a great job with it. You get a text-based layout that lists the time and date, the year and day in progress, your calendar, and a text-based app launcher list of favorites you set.

That’s the long and short of Indistractable Minimalist Launcher, and for anyone looking for a complete digital detox, this is what you want. Indistractable Minimalist Launcher looks like a throwback to an older age of computing, and that’s intentional. If you want the absolute bare minimum, with no distractions, install this launcher.

Also: How to turn on Private DNS Mode on Android – and why it’s a must for security.

At the moment, Indistractable Minimalist Launcher is in early access, so it’s free to install and use from the Google Play Store.

As for my current minimalist launcher of choice, I prefer Yin Yang Launcher for phones and the aforementioned AIO Launcher for tablets.

Industry News: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home.
  • According to recent reports, within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat.
  • The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

According to recent reports, within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.

The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.

Industry observers note that at least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit stated.

“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit noted. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”.

Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.

It has been revealed that “Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly noted. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”.

The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.

Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.

The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.

Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—remarked that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”.

The complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.

“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt noted. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”.

Recent findings suggest that all the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.

Car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, remarked his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”.

Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.

“The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield stated. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”.

In a recent development, the teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a canceled alert.

In a later investigation, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was canceled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.

Industry observers note that the OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct biannual trainings moving forward.

According to recent reports, they also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG said.

Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”.

It has been revealed that another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.

According to recent reports, these recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of whom remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report stated, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.

“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.

It has been revealed that the teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.

In a recent development, BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.

Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.

“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”.

Mitchell remarked that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.

Industry observers note that “In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell said. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a canceled alert must stay canceled.”.

Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The New York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”.

“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang stated.

According to recent reports, as a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she remarked.

“I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield said. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”.

Kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”.

Sources indicate that as AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release mentioned. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”.

The Move 2 is the most advanced Wi-Fi/Bluetooth hybrid speaker in Sonos’ lineup, with three Class-D amplifiers, two tweeters, and one midwoofer to back it up. This speaker’s acoustic structure is identical to that of the Era 100, so if you don’t need the Move 2’s portability, go with the Era 100.

#19892. Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1127 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
  • The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
  • Upgrade, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end consumers and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another massive provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Upgrade, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

According to recent reports, although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

According to recent reports, parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

It has been revealed that as noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

According to recent reports, last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically highlighted up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher noted he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

Industry observers note that the blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
  • In a recent development, the manufacturer’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta.
  • “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build newly introduced AI data centers.

In a recent development, the manufacturer’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”.

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the firm’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing fresh renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

In a recent development, but even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”.

It would very much be in the public interest for other Significant Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the fresh desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

Recent findings suggest that the search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

According to recent reports, the other massive change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

Sources indicate that it’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s fresh AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

Recent findings suggest that this change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

Introducing OpenAI

📅 11 Dec 2015 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, openAI is a non-profit artificial intelligence research company.
  • It has been revealed that we believe AI should be an extension of individual human wills and, in the spirit of liberty, as broadly and evenly distributed as possible.
  • Artificial intelligence has always been a surprising field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openAI is a non-profit artificial intelligence research company. Our goal is to advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return. Since our research is free from financial obligations, we can better focus on a positive human impact.

It has been revealed that we believe AI should be an extension of individual human wills and, in the spirit of liberty, as broadly and evenly distributed as possible. The outcome of this venture is uncertain and the work is difficult, but we believe the goal and the structure are right. We hope this is what matters most to the best in the field.

Artificial intelligence has always been a surprising field. In the early days, people thought that solving certain tasks (such as chess) would lead us to discover human-level intelligence algorithms. However, the solution to each task turned out to be much less general than people were hoping (such as doing a search over a huge number of moves).

The past few years have held another flavor of surprise. An AI technique explored for decades, deep learning, started achieving state-of-the-art results in a wide variety of problem domains. In deep learning, rather than hand-code a upcoming algorithm for each problem, you design architectures that can twist themselves into a wide range of algorithms based on the data you feed them.

This approach has yielded outstanding results on pattern recognition problems, such as recognizing objects in images, machine translation, and speech recognition. But we’ve also started to see what it might be like for computers to be creative⁠(opens in a fresh window), to dream⁠(opens in a new window), and to experience the world⁠(opens in a new window).

AI systems today have impressive but narrow capabilities. It seems that we’ll keep whittling away at their constraints, and in the extreme case they will reach human performance on virtually every intellectual task. It’s hard to fathom how much human-level AI could benefit society, and it’s equally hard to imagine how much it could damage society if built or used incorrectly.

In a recent development, because of AI’s surprising history, it’s hard to predict when human-level AI might come within reach. When it does, it’ll be notable to have a leading research institution which can prioritize a good outcome for all over its own self-interest.

According to recent reports, we’re hoping to grow OpenAI into such an institution. As a non-profit, our aim is to build value for everyone rather than shareholders. Researchers will be strongly encouraged to publish their work, whether as papers, blog posts, or code, and our patents⁠ (if any) will be shared with the world. We’ll freely collaborate with others across many institutions and expect to work with companies to research and deploy upcoming technologies.

Recent findings suggest that openAI’s research director is Ilya Sutskever⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), one of the world experts in machine learning. Our CTO is Greg Brockman⁠(opens in a new window), formerly the CTO of Stripe. The group’s other founding members are world-class research engineers and scientists: Trevor Blackwell⁠(opens in a new window), Vicki Cheung⁠(opens in a new window), Andrej Karpathy⁠(opens in a new window), Durk Kingma⁠(opens in a new window), John Schulman⁠(opens in a new window), Pamela Vagata⁠(opens in a new window), and Wojciech Zaremba⁠(opens in a new window). Pieter Abbeel, Yoshua Bengio, Alan Kay, Sergey Levine, and Vishal Sikka are advisors to the group. OpenAI’s co-chairs are Sam Altman and Elon Musk.

In a recent development, sam, Greg, Elon, Reid Hoffman, Jessica Livingston, Peter Thiel, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Infosys, and YC Research⁠(opens in a upcoming window) are donating to support OpenAI. In total, these funders have committed $1 billion, although we expect to only spend a tiny fraction of this in the next few years.

You can follow us on Twitter at @OpenAI⁠(opens in a new window).

#19886. Weight normalization: A simple reparameterization to accelerate training of deep neural networks

📅 25 Feb 2016 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (167 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Weight normalization: A simple reparameterization to accelerate training of deep neural networks

📅 25 Feb 2016 | ⏱️ 1 min read (167 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We present weight normalization: a reparameterization of the weight vectors in a neural network that decouples the length of those weight vectors from their direction. By reparameterizing the weights in this way we improve the conditioning of the optimization problem and we speed up convergence of stochastic gradient descent. Our reparameterization is inspired by batch normalization but does not introduce any dependencies between the examples in a minibatch. This means that our method can also be applied successfully to recurrent models such as LSTMs and to noise-sensitive applications such as deep reinforcement learning or generative models, for which batch normalization is less well suited. Although our method is much simpler, it still provides much of the speed-up of full batch normalization. In addition, the computational overhead of our method is lower, permitting more optimization steps to be taken in the same amount of time. We demonstrate the usefulness of our method on applications in supervised image recognition, generative modelling, and deep reinforcement learning.
